Matroid

Words: 46
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A matroid on a finite set E consists of a nonempty family of independent subsets closed under taking subsets and satisfying exchange: if independent sets I,J obey ∣I∣<∣J∣, some j∈J∖I has I∪{j} independent. Linear independence of vectors is the motivating example. A pregeometry is a finitary closure-theoretic extension to possibly infinite sets.

Rule of product (∣A1​×⋯×Ak​∣=∏j=1k​∣Aj​∣)

Words: 73
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For finite sets, the number of ordered choices of one element from each is the product of the individual numbers of choices. More generally, if stage j has exactly nj​ possible choices after every permitted history of earlier stages, the total number of full choice sequences is ∏j​nj​, by mathematical induction on the stages. This counts ba functions between sets of sizes a,b, and counts the injective functions by the falling factorial b(b−1)⋯(b−a+1) when a≤b.

Steiner system (S(t,k,v))

Words: 366 Articles: 5
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A Steiner system S(t,k,v) is a v-point set with k-point blocks such that every t-point subset is contained in exactly one block. Necessarily the number of blocks is (tv​)/(tk​). This count is a necessary consistency check, not a substitute for proving exact containment. The small Witt design is S(5,6,12).

Block of a Steiner system

Words: 37
Steiner system OurBigBook.com
A designated subset in a Steiner system is a Steiner block. In a system S(t,k,v), each Steiner block contains k points and each t-point subset belongs to exactly one Steiner block. For t=2, this is the pair-coverage condition used in a cyclotomic construction of a Steiner 2-design.

Difference family for a Steiner 2-design

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Steiner system OurBigBook.com
In a finite additive group, a family of k-subsets is a difference family of index one if each nonzero group element occurs exactly once among all their ordered within-block differences. Translating its Steiner blocks by every group element gives a Steiner system with parameters 2-(v,k,1): the unique representation of a difference determines the unique translated Steiner block through two specified points.

Cyclotomic construction of a Steiner 2-design

Words: 85
Difference family for a Steiner 2-design OurBigBook.com
Put m=(2k​), take odd q≡1(mod2m), and let H be the index-m multiplicative subgroup. If a k-set A has its unordered pair differences in distinct H-cosets, choose S⊂H containing exactly one element from each pair {h,−h}. Then {sA:s∈S} is a difference family for a Steiner 2-design. Indeed one unordered pair supplies each coset, and its two difference orientations multiplied by S cover that coset once. Translations yield a 2-(q,k,1) Steiner system. The cyclotomic pattern extension by a second-moment bound supplies suitable A for all sufficiently large q in this progression.

Small Witt design (S(5,6,12))

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Steiner system OurBigBook.com
The small Witt design is a Steiner system S(5,6,12) with 132 blocks. A six-set duad-syntheme duality constructs it on two disjoint six-sets: two whole-half blocks, forty-five blocks of each of the types (2,4) and (4,2), and forty corresponding-partition blocks of type (3,3). The internal-duad/cross-syntheme incidence rule proves that each five-set lies in exactly one of these blocks.

Synthematic construction of the small Witt design

Words: 75
Small Witt design OurBigBook.com
On a six-point set X and its six totals of synthemes Y, each duad determines a partition of Y into three pairs according to their shared synthemes. Include both whole halves, the 45 blocks D∪(Y∖P) for these duad-pair incidences, and their complements. For each partition X=A⊔Ac into triples, cross synthemes give two triangular components on Y; include the four unions of a part of X with a component. These 132 blocks form the small Witt design.

Six-point matching geometry

Words: 402 Articles: 6
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
The complete graph on six points has fifteen edges and fifteen perfect matchings. Its six one-factorizations organize a dual incidence geometry exchanging points with factorizations and edges with matchings. The classical names are duads, synthemes and totals of synthemes. This geometry supports duad-syntheme duality on six points and a construction of the small Witt design.

Pentad construction of the exceptional alternating-group automorphism

Words: 91
Six-point matching geometry OurBigBook.com
The six pentads are the six one-factorizations of the complete graph on six points. Permuting the ground-set points permutes these factorizations. The action sends a transposition to three disjoint transpositions and a 3-cycle to two disjoint 3-cycles. Its restriction to A6​ is faithful by simplicity, and the full action of S6​ is faithful because an order-two kernel would be central. It is consequently an automorphism of S6​. Its restriction preserves A6​ and changes 3-cycle type, so it cannot be induced on A6​ by any conjugation from S6​.

Duad-syntheme duality on six points

Words: 79
Six-point matching geometry OurBigBook.com
A bijection from the points of one six-set to the totals of another extends by incidence to bijections from duads to synthemes, synthemes to duads, and totals to points. A duad maps to the intersection of its two point-totals. The same duality exchanges internal duads of a three-versus-three partition with cross synthemes of its corresponding partition. The latter rule follows by splitting the six cross perfect matchings into parity classes of three, yielding two triangles on the six totals.

Duad

Words: 187 Articles: 3
Six-point matching geometry OurBigBook.com
A duad is an unordered pair of distinct points. On a six-point set there are (26​)=15 duads. They are the edges of the complete graph and are grouped into synthemes.

Syntheme

Words: 157 Articles: 2
Duad OurBigBook.com
A syntheme partitions six points into three duads, equivalently a perfect matching of the complete graph. There are 6!/(233!)=15 synthemes. Every duad belongs to three. Two edge-disjoint synthemes extend to a unique total of synthemes: their union is a six-cycle, whose complement has a unique factorization into three matchings.
Total of synthemes
Words: 109 Articles: 1
Syntheme OurBigBook.com
A total is a set of five edge-disjoint synthemes covering all fifteen duads of a six-point set. There are six totals; each syntheme belongs to two and every two totals share exactly one syntheme. Each total contains exactly one syntheme containing any prescribed duad. Totals are one-factorizations of the complete graph.
Counting synthematic totals
Words: 58
Total of synthemes OurBigBook.com
Two disjoint synthemes form a six-cycle, whose complement is a triangular prism. The prism has a unique partition into three perfect matchings, so the pair extends uniquely to a total of synthemes. Eight synthemes are disjoint from a fixed syntheme; grouping them four per total yields two totals through it, and double counting gives six totals in all.

Cycle lemma (∑i​bi​=1)

Words: 59
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
For an integer sequence with total sum one, exactly one cyclic starting position has every nonempty partial sum strictly positive. Starting after the last minimum of the proper partial sums proves existence. Two good starts would divide the sequence into two positive integer arc sums adding to one, proving uniqueness. This form counts cyclic prefix constraints in the cyclic Turán covering construction.

Cyclic digit run

Words: 64
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A cyclic digit run is a consecutive segment of a digit string whose successive digits all increase by one or all decrease by one modulo the base. For example, 8,9,0,1 is an increasing decimal run. This refers to cyclic digit values, not to joining the final position of the string back to its first position. Overlapping run constraints can be counted with the inclusion-exclusion principle.

Topological sorting

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Directed acyclic graph OurBigBook.com
A topological sorting constructs a topological order of a finite Directed acyclic graph. Repeatedly remove a vertex of indegree zero and place it next in the ordering. Such a vertex exists in every nonempty finite Directed acyclic graph, since otherwise following predecessor edges eventually creates a directed cycle.

Topological order

Words: 39
Topological sorting OurBigBook.com
A topological order is an ordering of a directed graph's vertices in which every arc points from an earlier vertex to a later one. A finite directed graph admits such an ordering exactly when it is a Directed acyclic graph.

Markov equivalence of directed acyclic graphs

Words: 126 Articles: 2
Directed acyclic graph OurBigBook.com
Two Directed acyclic graphs are Markov equivalent when they encode the same D-separations for all disjoint sets of vertices. They consequently impose the same global Markov property for a directed acyclic graph, although their causal interpretations can differ.

Completed partially directed acyclic graph

Words: 57
Markov equivalence of directed acyclic graphs OurBigBook.com
The completed partially directed acyclic graph of a Markov equivalence of directed acyclic graphs class has their common skeleton of a directed graph. An edge is directed exactly when its orientation agrees in every member of the class, and is otherwise undirected. It can be constructed by enumerating all acyclic orientations with the prescribed unshielded colliders and retaining only the common directions; practical PC algorithms use orientation propagation instead of enumeration.

Skeleton and collider characterization of Markov equivalence

Words: 42
Markov equivalence of directed acyclic graphs OurBigBook.com
Two Directed acyclic graphs are Markov equivalent directed acyclic graphs if and only if they have the same skeleton of a directed graph and the same unshielded colliders. Thus these two structures determine the observational equivalence class. This structural theorem is what converts the skeleton and collider phases of the PC algorithm into identification of an equivalence class.

Moral graph

Words: 49 Articles: 1
Directed acyclic graph OurBigBook.com
The moral graph of a Directed acyclic graph joins every pair of vertices with a common child and then replaces every directed edge by an undirected edge.

Hammersley-Clifford theorem

Words: 25
Moral graph OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive probability density, factorization into clique potentials of an undirected graph is equivalent to the global Markov conditional-independence property for that graph.

Topological ordering

Words: 18
Directed acyclic graph OurBigBook.com
A topological ordering places every parent before each child.
A topological sorting constructs such a topological order of a directed acyclic graph.

D-separation

Words: 145 Articles: 5
Directed acyclic graph OurBigBook.com
D-separation blocks paths through conditioned noncolliders and through unconditioned colliders without conditioned descendants.

Collider

Words: 73 Articles: 1
D-separation OurBigBook.com
On a path in a directed graph, an interior vertex is a collider when both adjacent path edges have arrowheads pointing into it. A path through a collider is blocked unless that collider or one of its descendants is conditioned upon.
Unshielded collider
Words: 32
Collider OurBigBook.com
An unshielded collider in a Directed acyclic graph is a triple a→b←c with a and c nonadjacent. The absence of an edge between its outer vertices makes this orientation detectable from conditional independence information under faithfulness of a directed acyclic graph.

D-separating set

Words: 13
D-separation OurBigBook.com
A set d-separates two vertex sets when it blocks every path between them.

Local Markov property of a directed acyclic graph

Words: 15
D-separation OurBigBook.com
Conditioned on its parents, a vertex is d-separated from all nondescendants other than those parents.

Global Markov property of a directed acyclic graph

Words: 31
D-separation OurBigBook.com
The global Markov property of a Directed acyclic graph says that d-separation of vertex sets A and B by S implies conditional independence of the corresponding random vectors given the variables at S.

Incidence geometry

Words: 1k Articles: 23
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Incidence geometry studies which points lie on which curves, lines or higher-dimensional objects and how many such incidences a finite configuration can have.

Linear space (geometry)

Words: 70
Incidence geometry OurBigBook.com
A linear space is a structure in incidence geometry with a set of points and a collection of subsets called lines: any two distinct points lie on exactly one line, and every line contains at least two points. The lines here are incidence-theoretic objects, without a required coordinate realization. A finite linear space imposes finiteness; its nontrivial form excludes a line containing all points. Pruning and minimal-degree polynomial argument
Words: 123
Joints theorem OurBigBook.com
Let a line collection have M joints of a line collection and put D=⌈nM1/n⌉. If M>LD, deleting each line with at most D current joints of a line collection, together with those joints of a line collection, leaves a nonempty configuration in which every line has more than D joints of a line collection. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most D vanishes on the retained joints of a line collection by rank-nullity theorem. Choose one of minimum degree. Its restriction vanishes identically on every retained line, so its gradient is orthogonal to a spanning set of directions at every joint of a line collection and hence vanishes there. Each nonzero partial derivative would be a lower-degree polynomial with the same zeros, contradicting minimality. In characteristic zero, all derivatives vanishing forces a constant polynomial, another contradiction. Therefore M≤LD, giving the joints theorem. The argument's characteristic-zero assumption is essential to its derivative step.

There is always a choice because the final entry is a root. These inverse operations give nn−k−1 choices for the earlier entries and k for the last. For k=n, the empty forest is unique.

For a labelled tree on n≥2 vertices, repeatedly delete the leaf with smallest label and record its neighbour, until two vertices remain. The recorded sequence has length n−2. Conversely, given such a sequence, repeatedly join its first label to the smallest remaining label absent from the remaining sequence, remove that latter vertex, and delete the first sequence entry. Finally join the two remaining vertices. These operations are inverse bijections between labelled trees and sequences of n−2 labels, proving the Cayley formula nn−2.

Refinement of a set partition

Words: 98
Set partition OurBigBook.com
A set partition Q refines P if every cell of Q is contained in a cell of P. Thus Q retains every separation made by P and may make additional separations. Refinement of a set partition is reflexive and transitive. If each partition refines the other, their cells coincide, so refinement of a set partition is a partial order on partitions. For finite partitions the nonempty intersections of cells form their common refinement of a set partition. In graph regularity arguments, subdividing cells and treating discarded vertices as singletons preserves refinement of a set partition; merging discarded vertices into one cell need not. The refinement variance identity for regularity energy consequently proves that this singleton treatment cannot decrease the equitable regularity energy.

The polynomial method in combinatorics encodes a discrete configuration by polynomials and obtains combinatorial bounds from their degree, zeros, coefficients, or linear independence.

Rich line covering bound over a finite field (∣N∣≥(nn+m−1​))

Words: 86
Polynomial method in combinatorics OurBigBook.com
Suppose every point of Fqn​ lies on an affine line in a vector space meeting a subset N in at least m points, with 1≤m≤q. A smaller N would admit a nonzero multivariate polynomial of total degree at most m−1 vanishing on it, by the dimension of a bounded-total-degree polynomial space. Each selected line then has more roots of a polynomial than the degree of its restriction, so the polynomial vanishes at every point. The Schwartz-Zippel lemma forbids this because m−1<q. Thus the displayed bound holds, and is at least mn/n!. This is a point-covering condition; the finite-field Kakeya set condition instead quantifies over directions.

For a nonzero multivariate polynomial of total degree d over a field, and a finite subset S of that field, at most d∣S∣n−1 points of Sn are zeros. For one variable this is the root bound for a polynomial. If d≥∣S∣, the bound is already trivial. Otherwise, in the inductive proof write the polynomial as degree k in its last variable, with a nonzero leading coefficient of degree at most d−k in the other variables. The leading coefficient vanishes on at most (d−k)∣S∣n−2 fibers; outside those fibers there are at most k roots of a polynomial per fiber. Counting the bad fibers with the trivial ∣S∣ bound gives the asserted inequality.

Symmetric function

Words: 722 Articles: 17
Combinatorics OurBigBook.com
A symmetric function is a formal power series of bounded total degree that is invariant under every finite permutation of its variables. Symmetric functions form a graded ring with several useful bases.

Cauchy identity for symmetric functions (∏i,j​(1−xi​yj​)−1=∑λ​sλ​(x)sλ​(y))

Words: 145 Articles: 2
Symmetric function OurBigBook.com
Expand each factor as a geometric series indexed by a nonnegative matrix. The RSK correspondence preserves its row and column contents, changing the sum to pairs of Semistandard Young tableaux of the same shape and proving the displayed formal identity. Its kernel is also ∑λ​hλ​(x)mλ​(y)=∑λ​pλ​(x)pλ​(y)/zλ​. These are dual-basis kernels for the Hall inner product of symmetric functions, so the Schur expansion proves orthonormality. Applying the symmetric-function involution in one alphabet gives the dual identity ∏i,j​(1+xi​yj​)=∑λ​sλ​(x)sλ′​(y).

Apply the symmetric-function involution in one alphabet to the ordinary Cauchy identity. It changes complete generators to elementary ones and, by the dual Jacobi–Trudi identity, sends sλ​ to sλ′​. This proves the identity as a formal series and relates pairings with transposed Young shapes to squarefree matrix weights.

Symmetric-function involution (ω(er​)=hr​,ω(pr​)=(−1)r−1pr​)

Words: 124 Articles: 1
Symmetric function OurBigBook.com
The Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials gives freely generated elementary functions, so sending each er​ to hr​ defines an algebra homomorphism. For E(t)=∑er​tr and H(t)=∑hr​tr, E(−t)H(t)=1. Applying the homomorphism shows ω(H(t))=E(t), hence ω2=1. Taking logarithms of H gives the displayed action on power sums. It preserves the Hall inner product of symmetric functions because each power-sum basis vector acquires only a sign.

Forgotten symmetric function (fλ​=(−1)∣λ∣−ℓ(λ)ω(mλ​))

Symmetric-function involution OurBigBook.com
The coefficient of mμ​ in fλ​ counts distinct rearrangements of the parts of λ whose prefix-sum set contains the prefix sums of μ. Indeed, Hall inner product of symmetric functions duality between mλ​,hλ​ turns this coefficient into (−1)∣λ∣−ℓ(λ) times the coefficient of hλ​ in eμ​. Expanding E(t)=H(−t)−1 expresses each eμj​​ as a signed sum of compositions of μj​. Concatenating these compositions gives precisely the counted rearrangements, and every sign is (−1)∣λ∣−ℓ(λ).

Monomial symmetric function (mλ​)

Words: 42
Symmetric function OurBigBook.com
For an integer partition λ, mλ​ sums the distinct monomials whose positive exponent multiset is λ. No multiplicity is attached to repeated parts. The functions of fixed total degree form a basis of the symmetric functions of that degree, since finite variable permutations identify precisely these monomial orbits.

Hall inner product of symmetric functions (⟨pα​,pβ​⟩=δαβ​zα​)

Words: 45
Symmetric function OurBigBook.com
Here pα​ is a product of power-sum symmetric functions and zα​=∏r​rmr​mr​! for part multiplicities mr​. The Frobenius characteristic map identifies this product with the ordinary character inner product. Schur functions are orthonormal, and the adjoint of multiplication by pk​ is k∂/∂pk​. These properties turn a power-sum multiplication formula into the Murnaghan–Nakayama rule.

Bialternant formula OurBigBook.com
Put bi​=λi​+N−i. In the bialternant formula, substitute xj​=etyj​ with distinct yj​ and compare the first nonzero determinant coefficients as t→0. They arise from the distinct degrees 0,…,N−1 in the exponential expansions. The common factor in the yj​ and the factorials cancel, leaving the product of differences of the bi​ divided by the differences of N−i. This proves the displayed integral specialization without dividing by a vanishing Vandermonde value.

Words: 38
Schur polynomial OurBigBook.com
Sum the weight monomials of all Semistandard Young tableaux on the skew Young diagram λ/μ, with weak rows and strict columns. A Bender-Knuth involution interchanges the counts of adjacent letters without changing the shape, so the sum is a symmetric function. Taking μ empty gives the Schur function.

Words: 49
Jacobi–Trudi identity OurBigBook.com
Here [a] is the trivial character of Sa​, [0] is the induction-product unit, [a]=0 for a<0, and multiplication is induction of external tensor products. The Frobenius characteristic map turns the expression into the Jacobi–Trudi identity. A sign-reversing involution on intersecting lattice-path systems leaves precisely the nonintersecting systems corresponding to Semistandard Young tableaux, proving the determinant identity.

For a partition of an integer λ⊢n, padded to m rows, let δ=(m−1,…,0). If a permutation has αq​ cycles of length q, put pα​=∏q​(∑i​xiq​)αq​. The character of the Specht module Sλ is the displayed coefficient. Equivalently pα​Aδ​=∑λ​χλ(α)Aλ+δ​, the alternant form of the Frobenius characteristic map. It gives finite coefficient computations without constructing representation matrices.
